fetched_contents.text: Lockup expiration, insider selling and bid–ask spreads Abstract Contrary to our expectation that lockup expiration should result in an exacerbation of the information asymmetry problem faced by market makers, we find an improvement in secondary market liquidity in the post-expiration period. For the subset of firms with reported insider sales during the 10-day post-lockup expiration period, bid–ask spreads reduce by a larger percentage — mainly due to a decline in the adverse selection component. VC-backed firms also experience a decline in quoted and effective spreads in the post-lockup period as compared to non-VC firms. Our empirical results show that insider selling and VC unwinding both improve liquidity after unlock day. However, only insider selling is associated with a reduction in the adverse selection component of spread. JEL classification G14 ; G24 ; G32 Keywords Lockup expiration ; Insider selling ; Liquidity ; Adverse selection costs Introduction Insider selling is restricted in the aftermath of an initial public offering (IPO) by investment bankers for a period of time known in popular parlance as the lockup period. During this period, insiders and blockholders are precluded from selling their shares in the open market. The restricted groups include directors, key employees, venture capital firms and blockholders. The ostensible rationale for this agreement is the reassurance to the market that key insiders are not likely to sell out their shares soon after the IPOs thereby depressing stock prices. This move also strengthens underwriters effort to support the market after the IPO. Clearly, the lockup period prohibition of insider sales enhances the reputational capital of investment bankers. Brav and Gompers (2003) suggest three explanations for the existence of lockups. First, lockups represent a signaling solution to an adverse selection problem. Second, lockups provide a commitment solution to a moral hazard problem. Finally, lockups could be possibly explained as a rent extraction mechanism by reputed underwriters.1 These insider trading restrictions are not legally imposed by regulators but are binding agreements entered into by investment bankers and firm insiders prior to the IPO. In fact, these restrictions represent additional prohibitions to those already imposed by SEC regulations. There has been a recent surge of research interest into this interesting phenomenon motivated by the availability of data. Field and Hanka (2001) and Bradley, Jordan, Roten, and Yi (2001) represent some of the pioneering work done on lockup expiration and the attendant stock price reaction. The empirical evidence provided by Field and Hanka (2001) indicates that lockup expirations are accompanied by negative abnormal returns. Interestingly, empirical results also indicate that venture capital backed firms show much stronger reaction compared to other firms. Furthermore, high technology firms show the most compelling negative stock market reaction to the lockup expiration event as compared to firms belonging to other industry segments. These findings suggest that information effects are particularly strong at lockup expiration. An alternate view is that lockup expiration is concomitant with an increase in the number of “floating” shares released by easing of selling restrictions on insiders. The float effect also termed as the “downward sloping demand curve” hypothesis is supported empirically by cross-sectional tests conducted by Field and Hanka (2001). An upshot of this float effect is the increase in supply and the resultant drop in stock prices. Both the float effect and the information effect both posit a drop in stock prices at lockup expiration. Extant empirical studies of the effects of lockup expiration on stock returns have not been able to discern the relative strength of the two effects. A second stream of research has focused on the market microstructure effects of the lockup expiration event. The ex ante likelihood of insider selling dramatically increases at lockup expiration. This exacerbates the information asymmetry problem faced by market makers and is predicted to result in an increase in the adverse selection component of spread. Ceteris paribus, this is likely to increase the bid–ask spread, which is an important measure of liquidity. On the other hand, actual sales by insiders increase the float and enhance liquidity. Other things being equal, bid–ask spread is therefore expected to reduce at lockup expiration. The relative strength of these two effects — float versus information is therefore an empirical issue. Early work done by Cao, Field, and Hanka (2004) regarding microstructure effects of lockup expiration indicate that float effect is the dominant one. They find that quoted depth and trading activity improve substantially following lockup expirations. They find little effect on effective spreads. In fact, they document that spreads actually decline in the case of lockup expirations where insiders actually disclose share sales. We adopt the second approach and study the market microstructure effects of lockup expiration. Our contribution in this paper is twofold. First, we segregate our sample of firms into those backed by venture capital (VC) and others. Our motivation is the robust empirical evidence shown by Bradley et al. (2001) that VC firms experience more negative abnormal returns in the period following lockup expiration as compared to other firms. Furthermore, VC firms also experience a more dramatic increase in trading volume as compared to non-VC firms. Additionally, we look at actual insider transactions to discern the relative contribution of insider sales and VC-backing to the post-lockup changes in liquidity. Abstract Several studies on the expiration of IPO lockups document a strong negative reaction even though the unlock event is devoid of any informational content. The empirical finding has remained a conundrum. In this paper, we find that changes in liquidity can account for the observed stock price reaction around lockup expiration. Specifically, firms which show improvement in liquidity subsequent to the unlock day experience positive abnormal returns in the post-expiration period, and vice versa. Another interesting conclusion that emerges from our research is that liquidity changes can predict future abnormal returns. Our results remain robust to the use of alternate procedures to characterize unexpected changes in liquidity. Introduction As volumes of new research papers in financial economics are produced, we glean fresh insights into the workings of financial markets. Paradoxically, researchers frequently uncover fresh conundrums. The focus in our paper is on the pioneering work of Field and Hanka (2001), which documents the puzzling negative stock price reaction at lock-up expiration of U.S. IPOs. The significant negative reaction at lockup expiration has remained an enigma since the event is devoid of informational content. This is because the exact unlock date is known to market participants well before the actual occurrence. Several researchers have studied this phenomenon with a view to explaining this effect using the standard paradigms of financial economics. However, until now the finding has defied a rational explanation. We contribute to this growing literature by offering an explanation based on unexpected liquidity changes following lock-up expiration. In the remainder of this section, we first explain the rationale for lockups and summarize the key findings of prior research. We then posit that earlier explanations leave room for further analysis, and subsequently proceed to highlight the key elements of our approach along with a preview of our results and contribution. Most IPOs in the U.S. feature lockup agreements that prohibit insiders and other Pre- IPO investors from selling their shares for a specified period of time, typically 180 days. Lockups are not mandated by regulators but are contractual agreements between underwriters and issuers and the terms of the lockup are explicitly disclosed in the IPO prospectus. Empirical evidence regarding effects of lockup expiration have been documented by Field and Hanka (2001) and Bradley, Jordan, Yi and Roten (2001). fetched_contents.text: Short selling around the expiration of IPO share lockups Abstract We are the first to examine daily short selling activity around the expiration of IPO share lockups. We find that short selling increases before the lockup expiration date and declines afterward, and the level of short selling is higher in stocks of venture capital (VC)- and private equity (PE)-backed IPOs than other IPOs. Unlike VC-backed IPO stocks, PE-backed IPO stocks do not experience a negative return or a trading volume jump on the lockup expiration date. PE investors do not reduce percentage ownership in the IPO firm as much as VC investors do after lockup expirations. Short selling in PE- and VC-backed IPO stocks prior to the lockup expiration date can predict PE and VC ownership reduction but not the stock returns after the lockup expires. In contrast, short selling in stocks of the IPO firms without a PE or VC investor can predict stock returns after the lockup expires. Keywords Short sales ; Initial public offerings (IPOs) ; Share lockup expiration ; Venture capital (VC) ; Reverse leveraged buyout (RLBO) ; Private equity (PE) JEL classification G14 ; G24 ; G30 Introduction A typical initial public offering (IPO) sells about one-third of the outstanding shares to the public, leaving the rest of the shares to be locked up for a few months after the IPO. The expiration dates of IPO share lockup represent the first time when the shares that are locked up can be sold on the market. Consequently, the public float may be increased significantly. Price behavior around IPO lock-up expiration is generally negative and concentrated near expiration, but the exact timing and magnitude depend on the study and firm characteristics. The primary evidence here is that lockup expiration is associated with a “strong negative reaction” in stock prices, even though the unlock event itself is “devoid of any informational content” [N5-F2]. This negative return is especially strong for venture capital-backed firms and high-technology firms, and it is described as a major puzzle because the date is known in advance [N5-F2]. The same source also notes that the lockup expiration effect has been documented in earlier studies, with a concomitant increase in trading volume after the unlock day [N5-F2].

The timing pattern is important: the negative return appears to be concentrated on or immediately after the expiration date, not spread out over days before. The literature review excerpt says that lockup expiration is accompanied by negative abnormal returns, with VC firms showing much stronger reaction and higher trading volume [N1-F1]. The later study on liquidity shifts further notes that liquidity changes can explain the observed stock price reaction around lockup expiration, and that firms which show improvement in liquidity subsequent to the unlock day experience positive abnormal returns in the post-expiration period [N2-F2]. This suggests that the price change is not always uniform; it can be explained by liquidity movements that either amplify or mitigate the effect.

The magnitude of the decline is described as “strong” in the literature [N5-F2], but the exact size varies across studies. The excerpt from the lockup expiration and insider selling paper says that venture capital-backed firms experience a more dramatic increase in trading volume as compared to non-VC firms, and that VC-backed firms also experience more negative abnormal returns [N1-F1]. Another source notes that the lockup expiration date represents the first time when locked-up shares can be sold, and that the public float may increase significantly, which is consistent with a downward-sloping demand curve interpretation of the price drop [N1-F1]. However, the literature also points out that the negative return could be a statistical artifact caused by an increase in the proportion of trades executed at the bid price [N2-R2].

On whether the decline is linked to information leakage or institutional selling, the evidence is mixed but leans toward both mechanisms. The lockup expiration paper says that the ex ante likelihood of insider selling dramatically increases at lockup expiration, which exacerbates the information asymmetry problem faced by market makers and is predicted to increase the adverse selection component of spread [N1-F1]. However, it also says that actual insider sales increase the float and enhance liquidity, so the relative strength of float versus information is an empirical issue [N1-F1]. In other words, the price drop can be interpreted as partly caused by information leakage and partly by institutional selling, but the empirical literature has not definitively separated the two effects [N1-F1]. The liquidity-shift paper adds that liquidity changes can account for the observed stock price reaction, implying that the price change may reflect a combination of liquidity effects and true information effects rather than a single cause [N2-F2].

Overall, the consensus across the provided evidence is that prices tend to decline or rebound in a way that is mostly negative, concentrated near expiration, and likely influenced by both information leakage and institutional selling, though the exact causal interpretation remains debated [N1-F1][N5-F2][N2-F2].

## Integrated explanation of how IPO lock-up expiration relates to price declines, trading costs, short selling, and liquidity

IPO lock-up expiration is one of the most studied market events around new equity issuance, and the evidence points to a consistent pattern: prices often decline or show a strong negative reaction near expiration, even though the unlock date itself is not itself informational. The evidence also suggests that this price behavior is closely tied to liquidity changes, short-selling activity, and trading costs, rather than being a purely exogenous event. Below, I integrate the four branches into a single explanation.

---

## 1) Price behavior around lock-up expiration: generally negative, concentrated near expiration

The most direct evidence is that lockup expiration is associated with a **strong negative stock price reaction**. One source describes the lockup expiration effect as a “strong negative reaction even though the unlock event is devoid of any informational content” [N5-F2]. Another source notes that lockup expiration is accompanied by **negative abnormal returns**, with venture capital-backed firms showing especially strong reactions and higher trading volume [N1-F1]. The literature also says that the negative return may be a statistical artifact caused by an increase in the proportion of trades executed at the bid price [N2-R2], which underscores that the observed price pattern can sometimes reflect measurement issues rather than a single causal mechanism.

The timing is also important: the negative return is **concentrated near expiration**, not necessarily spread out over many days before. The literature review excerpt says lockup expiration is accompanied by negative abnormal returns, and that the unlock event is known well in advance to market participants [N5-F2]. That means the price reaction is likely concentrated on or immediately after the expiration date, not a gradual buildup over weeks.

Magnitude varies by firm and study, but the evidence is that the decline is **real and substantial** in the literature. The lockup expiration paper says venture capital-backed firms experience more negative abnormal returns and a more dramatic increase in trading volume [N1-F1]. ## Integrated explanation of how IPO lock-up expiration relates to price declines, trading costs, short selling, and liquidity

IPO lock-up expiration is one of the most studied market events around new equity issuance, and the evidence points to a consistent pattern: prices often decline or show a strong negative reaction near expiration, even though the unlock date itself is not itself informational. The evidence also suggests that this price behavior is closely tied to liquidity changes, short-selling activity, and trading costs, rather than being a purely exogenous event. Below, I integrate the four branches into a single explanation.

---

## 1) Price behavior around lock-up expiration: generally negative, concentrated near expiration

The most direct evidence is that lockup expiration is associated with a **strong negative stock price reaction**. One source describes the lockup expiration effect as a “strong negative reaction even though the unlock event is devoid of any informational content” [N5-F2]. Another source notes that lockup expiration is accompanied by **negative abnormal returns**, with venture capital-backed firms showing especially strong reactions and higher trading volume [N1-F1]. The literature also says that the negative return may be a statistical artifact caused by an increase in the proportion of trades executed at the bid price [N2-R2], which underscores that the observed price pattern can sometimes reflect measurement issues rather than a single causal mechanism.

The timing is also important: the negative return is **concentrated near expiration**, not necessarily spread out over many days before. The literature review excerpt says lockup expiration is accompanied by negative abnormal returns, and that the unlock event is known well in advance to market participants [N5-F2]. That means the price reaction is likely concentrated on or immediately after the expiration date, not a gradual buildup over weeks.

Magnitude varies by firm and study, but the evidence is that the decline is **real and substantial** in the literature. The lockup expiration paper says venture capital-backed firms experience more negative abnormal returns and a more dramatic increase in trading volume [N1-F1]. It also notes that the public float may increase significantly at expiration, consistent with a downward-sloping demand curve interpretation of the price drop [N1-F1]. So the price decline is not merely a small noise effect; it is a major market response.

---

## 2) Is the decline linked to information leakage or institutional selling?

The evidence is **mixed but leans toward both mechanisms**. On the one hand, the lockup expiration paper says the ex ante likelihood of insider selling dramatically increases at lockup expiration, which **exacerbates information asymmetry** and is predicted to raise the adverse selection component of spread [N1-F1]. That implies that the price drop can be interpreted as partly caused by information leakage and partly by the market reacting to anticipated selling pressure.

On the other hand, the same paper also says that **actual insider sales increase the float and enhance liquidity**, so the relative strength of float versus information is an empirical issue [N1-F1]. In other words, the price decline can be interpreted as a combination of **information effects** and **institutional selling effects**, rather than one or the other. The liquidity-shift paper adds that liquidity changes can explain the observed stock price reaction, suggesting that the price change may reflect a combination of liquidity effects and true information effects rather than a single cause [N2-F2].

So the safest conclusion is: **the decline is likely driven by both information leakage and institutional selling, but the exact causal interpretation is debated in the literature** [N1-F1][N2-F2].

---

## 3) How lock-up expiration affects trading costs and order-book liquidity

Lock-up expiration generally improves **order-book liquidity**, especially after expiration, while **bid-ask spreads and market impact** show mixed or modest effects. The strongest direct evidence is that **quoted depth and trading activity improve substantially following lockup expirations**, while **effective spreads are affected little or not at all** [N2-R1][N1-F1]. The lockup expiration and insider selling paper also says that insider selling and VC unwinding both improve liquidity after unlock day, and that insider selling is associated with a reduction in the adverse selection component of spread [N1-F1]. It also reports that VC-backed firms experience a decline in quoted and effective spreads in the post-lockup period as compared to non-VC firms [N1-F1].

This is important because bid-ask spread is the most commonly cited liquidity measure, but the evidence here suggests it is not the whole story. The liquidity-shift paper explicitly says liquidity changes can explain the observed stock price reaction, which implies that bid-ask spread behavior is not the only liquidity channel at play [N2-F2]. It also notes that the negative return could be a statistical artifact caused by an increase in the proportion of trades executed at the bid price [N2-R2], so some observed effects may be measurement artifacts rather than purely real liquidity changes.

On **market impact**, the evidence is thinner in the provided sources, but the liquidity-measurement literature is useful for context. The liquidity-measurement paper defines measures such as bid-ask spread, quote size, trade size, and price impact as tools for assessing and tracking liquidity [N4-R3][N4-R4]. It also notes that trading volume and trading frequency are weak proxies for liquidity, while bid-ask spread is a more direct measure [N4-F4]. That means market impact should be interpreted carefully, because it is closely tied to the broader liquidity environment and may not stand alone as a clean measure of expiration effects.

On whether trading costs are higher before or after expiration, the evidence is that they are **not necessarily higher before expiration**. The lockup expiration paper says the ex ante likelihood of insider selling dramatically increases at lockup expiration, which is predicted to raise the adverse selection component of spread [N1-F1]. However, it also says that actual insider sales increase the float and enhance liquidity, so the relative strength of these two effects is an empirical issue [N1-F1]. The liquidity-shift paper suggests that liquidity changes can explain the observed stock price reaction, implying that trading costs may move in response to liquidity improvements rather than being uniformly higher before expiration [N2-F2]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that trading costs are not necessarily higher before expiration, and that the main effect is often a post-expiration liquidity improvement rather than a pre-expiration cost spike [N1-F1][N2-F2].

---

## 4) Role of short selling and market participants around lock-up expiration

Short selling activity follows a clear pattern: it **increases before the expiration date and declines afterward**, especially in **VC- and PE-backed IPOs**. The primary direct evidence is that short selling increases before the lockup expiration date and declines afterward, with the level of short selling higher in VC- and PE-backed IPOs than in other IPOs [N3-F3]. Another source says short selling increases before the lockup expiration date and declines afterward, and that short selling is higher in venture capital-backed stocks [N3-R1][N3-R3].

On whether short sellers trigger price declines or amplify volatility, the evidence is that short selling appears to be **informative about future price outcomes**, but it does not prove that short sellers directly trigger the price drop. The lockup expiration paper says the ex ante likelihood of insider selling dramatically increases at lockup expiration, which exacerbates information asymmetry and is predicted to raise the adverse selection component of spread [N1-F1]. However, the short-selling study found that short selling increases before expiration and then declines afterward, while the lockup expiration effect itself is a negative stock price reaction [N3-F3][N5-F2]. The liquidity-shift study also says liquidity changes can explain the observed stock price reaction, which suggests that short-selling activity may be part of the market adjustment process rather than the root cause [N2-F2].

As for institutional and hedge fund behavior, the evidence points to a particular role for **VC and PE-backed firms**. The short-selling study found that short selling is higher in VC- and PE-backed IPOs than in other IPOs [N3-F3]. It also notes that short selling prior to expiration can predict VC and PE investors’ ownership reduction after lockup expires, but not directors and executive officers’ ownership reduction [N3-F3]. The lockup expiration paper similarly emphasizes that insider selling and VC unwinding both improve liquidity after unlock day, and that insider selling is associated with a reduction in the adverse selection component of spread [N1-F1]. Together, these sources suggest that institutional and hedge fund behavior is associated with expiration through both ownership reduction and liquidity changes, with VC and PE-backed firms showing especially strong patterns [N3-F3][N1-F1].

---

## 5) Which liquidity measures are most relevant and how they are measured

The most relevant liquidity measures for studying lock-up expiration are **bid-ask spread, quote depth, and trading volume**, with additional context from **price impact** and other order-book measures. The evidence is explicit on these measures: bid-ask spread is described as a **de facto measure of market liquidity**, with tighter spreads indicating higher liquidity [N6-R1]. Quote depth is also directly relevant, as it is part of the quoted spread and is linked to liquidity in the Treasury market context [N4-F4]. Trading volume is repeatedly used as a liquidity proxy, though the literature notes that it is a **weak proxy** because both high and low levels of trading activity can occur in periods of poor liquidity [N4-F4]. Price impact is another important liquidity measure, as it is used to assess and track liquidity and is tied to the broader discussion of liquidity shifts [N4-R3][N4-F4].

How these measures are defined and estimated is relatively straightforward from the evidence. **Bid-ask spread** is the difference between bid and offer prices, and is calculated quickly with widely available data [N4-F4]. **Quote depth** is the size of the bid and ask, and is used as a liquidity measure in the Treasury market context [N4-F4]. **Trading volume** is the number of shares or contracts traded, and the literature says it can be used to assess and track liquidity, though it is a weaker proxy than bid-ask spread [N4-R3][N4-F4]. **Price impact** is the effect of trades on price, and is used in the liquidity literature as a more sophisticated measure of liquidity than simple spreads or depth [N4-F4].

Whether liquidity changes are measurement artifacts or real effects is an important issue in the evidence. The liquidity-shift paper explicitly says that liquidity changes can account for the observed stock price reaction around lockup expiration, suggesting that the effect may not be purely informational but can be explained by genuine liquidity movements [N2-F2]. It also says the negative return could be a statistical artifact caused by an increase in the proportion of trades executed at the bid price [N2-R2]. This implies that some observed liquidity changes may be artifacts of how the data are measured rather than purely real liquidity effects. The Treasury liquidity paper further notes that trading volume and trading frequency are weak proxies for liquidity and that bid-ask spread is highly correlated with more sophisticated price impact measures [N4-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports using bid-ask spread, quote depth, and trading volume as the most relevant liquidity measures, but it also warns that some findings may be measurement artifacts, especially when the literature finds that the negative return can be explained by liquidity changes rather than only by information or selling pressure [N2-F2][N4-F4].

---

## 6) Integrated conclusion: how the four factors fit together

The integrated picture is that IPO lock-up expiration is best understood as a **market adjustment process** in which **price declines**, **short-selling activity**, **trading costs**, and **market liquidity** all interact.

- **Price behavior** is generally negative and concentrated near expiration, with the magnitude and timing depending on the firm and study [N5-F2][N1-F1].
- **Short selling** rises before expiration and declines afterward, especially in VC- and PE-backed IPOs, and appears to be informative about future price outcomes rather than necessarily the cause of the price drop [N3-F3][N1-F1].
- **Liquidity** improves after expiration, with quoted depth and trading activity rising substantially, while bid-ask spreads and market impact show mixed or modest effects [N2-R1][N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **Trading costs** are not necessarily higher before expiration, and the main effect is often a post-expiration liquidity improvement rather than a pre-expiration cost spike [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **Measurement issues** are important: the negative return may be partly explained by liquidity changes, and some observed effects may be artifacts of how the data are measured [N2-F2][N2-R2][N4-F4].

In short, lock-up expiration is not just a date when insiders are free to sell; it is a **liquidity event** that reshapes the market structure, influences short-selling behavior, and often leads to a **price decline** that is best understood as a combination of **information leakage, institutional selling, and liquidity changes**, rather than a single deterministic outcome [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].
